title: StubHub's Profit Engine Roars Even as Revenue and EPS Miss; Shares Down 60% This Year
text:
StubHub's Profit Engine Roars Even as Revenue and EPS Miss; Shares Down 60% This Year — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers StubHub's Profit Engine Roars Even as Revenue and EPS Miss; Shares Down 60% This Year
 Add preferred source StubHub reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $124 million, up 84% with a record 25% margin, but revenue of $502 million and adjusted EPS of $0.05 missed estimates. The company raised full-year GMS guidance to 11%-13% growth while merely reiterating EBITDA guidance of $400 million to $420 million, leaving little room for a Q4 beat. Debt was extended to 2033, net leverage fell to 2.5 times and Moody's upgraded the rating to B2. Advertising and open distribution remain slow to scale, and management flagged World Cup, MLB playoff and concert on-sale timing as Q4 comparison risks. The stock trades near its 52-week low. Key Elements 
 StubHub Holdings Eric Baker Connie James Mike Noonan Evercore ISI TripAdvisor World Cup Moody's Live Nation National Football League Big 12 Conference StubHub Holdings (STUB) delivered a quarter on Nov. 10 in which the bottom-line engine outran the top line. Adjusted EBITDA climbed 84% to $124 million on a 25% margin, the widest the company has posted since going public, while revenue of $502 million and adjusted earnings per share of $0.05 both fell short of analyst expectations. The stock, which trades around $5.47, is down roughly 72% over the past year and sits about 8% above its 52-week low of $5.07.
 The divergence between profit and growth was the central tension of the quarter. Gross merchandise sales came in at $2.62 billion, up 7% and in line with estimates, but revenue missed consensus by about 2% and adjusted EPS fell 37.5% short of the $0.08 consensus. Investors have now seen two consecutive quarters of EPS misses after Q2 came in at $0.00 against a $0.24 estimate.
 Metric Q3 2026 Year-over-year change 
 GMS $2.62B +7% 
 Revenue $502M +7% 
 Adjusted EBITDA $124M +84% 
 Adjusted EBITDA margin 25% +10 pts 
 Adjusted EPS $0.05 Missed $0.08 estimate 
 Sales and marketing (% of revenue) 45% -9 pts 
 Note: Figures reflect adjusted, non-GAAP measures as reported by the company.
 The margin story rests largely on marketing discipline. Sales and marketing expense fell to 45% of revenue, a 9-point improvement, which management attributed to scale advantages and better conversion on channels including Google. Gross margin rose 2 points to 85%, helped by lower fulfillment costs once the World Cup concluded. Chief Executive Eric Baker described the quarter as reinforcing "the continued strength of consumer demand for live experiences" and StubHub's leadership in the resale market.
 Guidance offered a split verdict. The company lifted its full-year GMS outlook to $10.175 billion to $10.375 billion, implying 11% to 13% growth, from a prior 10% to 12% range. But it merely reiterated adjusted EBITDA guidance of $400 million to $420 million. Evercore ISI noted that the Street's Q4 EBITDA estimate of $116 million sits near the top of the implied $98 million to $118 million range, leaving little cushion for an upside surprise.
 On the balance sheet, the picture has improved markedly. StubHub repaid $100 million of debt in July, bringing total repayment since its IPO to $1.1 billion, and extended its term loan maturities by 3.5 years to October 2033 while trimming borrowing costs by 25 basis points. Moody's upgraded the corporate family rating to B2 from B3 in September. Gross debt stands at about $1.3 billion, with no maturities until 2033, and net leverage has fallen to 2.5 times from 4.5 times at the end of 2025.
 "Our net leverage was further reduced by half a turn to two and a half times at quarter end," Chief Financial Officer Connie James said on the earnings call. She added that the company generated $192 million of trailing-twelve-month free cash flow, a 53% conversion of adjusted EBITDA, or 77% excluding working-capital timing and interest costs.
 James will hand the finance reins to Mike Noonan, currently CFO of TripAdvisor, in January. Baker credited her with bringing "real discipline" to the balance sheet and capital markets activity.
 Two expansion bets are moving more slowly than the market had hoped. Advertising and open distribution, the initiatives meant to widen the addressable market beyond core resale, remain in product-fitting mode. Management expects advertising revenue to stay "immaterial" in 2026, in the tens of millions of dollars. Baker said the priority this year has been getting the self-serve experience right before scaling, and pointed to a forthcoming partnership with the Big 12 Conference covering football and basketball as evidence of supply-side momentum. He also praised the NFL's move toward open distribution of season-ticket resale across more marketplaces, calling it a strong validation of the model, though he declined to say whether StubHub would join that specific program.
 The regulatory backdrop has been supportive. Price-cap legislation failed to advance in California in August after New York declined to move a similar proposal earlier in the year. Baker noted that the subsegment regulators tend to target, resellers listing large volumes of high-demand concert inventory well above face value, accounted for roughly 10% of global GMS in 2025.
 The fourth quarter carries unusual noise. Management flagged the anniversary of the first general World Cup ticket release last December, a Major League Baseball postseason that featured two of the smallest markets and a five-game World Series, and the uncertainty of when promoters schedule major 2027 concert on-sales. Baker said underlying growth excluding those factors would run in the high single digits. Consensus EPS for the December quarter is $0.61.
 The setup leaves investors weighing a record margin against a stock near its lows. Bulls point to EBITDA margins at all-time highs, debt pushed out to 2033 and a valuation well below analyst targets. Bears note persistent revenue and EPS misses, unchanged EBITDA guidance and slow-scaling new revenue streams. A break below $5.07 would mark a fresh 52-week low, and with the shares only about 8% above that level, the Q4 report, and whether EBITDA lands in the upper half of the implied range, is likely to be the next real test.
